title: Abdominal X-ray: bowel obstruction and sigmoid volvulus

header.contentArea: Applied surgical science and critical care
guidelineVersions: James & Kelly, The abdominal radiograph, Ulster Med J (2013)

related.why: Small bowel obstruction and its management
Lactate and acidosis in obstructed bowel

brief.scenario: Mr Albert Finch, 81, lives in a care home and has long-standing constipation. He has 3 days of abdominal distension and hasn't passed flatus for 2 days. He has vomited once. Pulse 96, BP 134/78, temperature 36.9°C.
brief.task: The examiner will read out the findings of his abdominal X-ray, then give you other results. Interpret them and describe your management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Interpret the X-ray findings in order, name the pattern, look for danger, then decompress or operate.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling it 'large bowel obstruction' and missing the volvulus, or scoping a patient with peritonitis.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "This is a supine abdominal radiograph of Mr Finch, taken today."

grid.label: Systematic interpretation
grid.fail: Names a diagnosis without checking the patient, date or projection.
grid.pass: Patient, date, supine projection, adequacy; then works through bowel gas, diameters, free gas, soft tissues, calcification and bones.
grid.high: Asks for an erect chest film if perforation is possible, and asks whether Rigler's sign is present.

grid.label: Recognising sigmoid volvulus
grid.fail: Calls it large bowel obstruction or pseudo-obstruction without naming the volvulus.
grid.pass: Interprets the hugely dilated, featureless inverted-U loop arising from the pelvis as the coffee bean sign of sigmoid volvulus.
grid.high: Notes the proximal colon is dilated too, and that volvulus is a closed loop at risk of ischaemia.

grid.label: Small vs large bowel: the 3/6/9 rule
grid.fail: Can't tell small from large bowel.
grid.borderline: Knows the 3, 6 and 9 cm limits but can't describe the folds.
grid.pass: Small bowel: central, valvulae across the full width, dilated over 3 cm. Large bowel: peripheral, haustra partway across, over 6 cm, caecum over 9 cm.
grid.high: Knows gas in the rectum argues against complete mechanical obstruction; it can be seen in pseudo-obstruction or incomplete obstruction. Knows plain films rarely show the cause.

grid.label: Looking for ischaemia or perforation (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Doesn't examine for peritonism or ask for a lactate.
grid.pass: Examines for peritonism; bloods with blood gas and lactate; CT if the diagnosis is uncertain or ischaemia or perforation is suspected.
grid.high: Knows ischaemia can exist without a raised lactate, so clinical signs still decide.

grid.label: Resuscitation
grid.fail: Sends him for endoscopy without resuscitating.
grid.pass: ABCDE; IV access, fluids; nasogastric tube if vomiting; catheter and fluid balance; senior informed.
grid.high: Asks early about frailty, baseline function and wishes, which shape later decisions.

grid.label: Endoscopic decompression
grid.fail: Plans a laparotomy first, or a blind flatus tube only.
grid.pass: No ischaemia or perforation: flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression, inspecting the mucosa; leaves a flatus tube.
grid.high: Quotes success in 60–95%; knows dusky mucosa at endoscopy means stop and go to theatre.

grid.label: Indications for surgery (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Scopes a patient with peritonitis or perforation.
grid.pass: Urgent resection if detorsion fails, or the colon is non-viable or perforated.
grid.high: Plans with the consultant and anaesthetist; consents for resection and a possible stoma.

grid.label: Preventing recurrence
grid.fail: Discharges him after decompression with no plan.
grid.pass: Discusses sigmoid colectomy after decompression, ideally on the same admission.
grid.high: Quotes recurrence of 43–75%; endoscopic fixation if surgery is too risky; involves the patient and family.

failures.move: Attempting endoscopic decompression in a patient with peritonitis or perforation.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: delays resection of gangrenous or perforated colon.

failures.move: Not examining for peritonism or checking lactate before decompression.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: ischaemia is missed and the wrong treatment chosen.

failures.move: Calling it large bowel obstruction without naming volvulus.
failures.consequence: The closed-loop emergency and endoscopic decompression are missed.
It is likely to recur, each time risking ischaemia or perforation.

recovery.when: You named the pattern before checking details
recovery.line: Let me start properly: patient, date, projection, then the gas pattern.

recovery.when: You're unsure between volvulus and pseudo-obstruction
recovery.line: I'd ask for a CT to confirm and look for ischaemia.

knowledge.fact: Small bowel: central, valvulae conniventes cross the lumen, abnormal over 3 cm. Colon: peripheral, haustra don't cross fully; over 6 cm, caecum over 9 cm.
Sigmoid volvulus: inverted-U loop from the pelvis, coffee bean sign.
No ischaemia or perforation: flexible endoscopic decompression first, then a flatus tube.
Failed detorsion, non-viable or perforated colon: urgent resection.
Recurrence 43–75% after detorsion: offer sigmoid colectomy, ideally the same admission.

recall.think: A closed loop that can become gangrenous or perforate.
recall.say: "Coffee bean sign: sigmoid volvulus. Any sign of ischaemia?"
do: Interpret the X-ray findings in order
Peritonism, lactate, CT if in doubt
Scope and flatus tube, or theatre
recall.trap: A normal lactate doesn't exclude ischaemia.
recall.finish: Sigmoid colectomy, ideally on the index admission.

sources.name: James B, Kelly B. The abdominal radiograph. Ulster Med J 2013;82(3):179-187
sources.supports: A logical, repeatable step-by-step approach; single supine film for the acute abdomen, erect chest film if perforation suspected (RCR iRefer); small bowel central, with valvulae conniventes traversing the lumen; haustral folds don't span the colon; small bowel should not exceed 3 cm; large bowel peripheral with haustra; colon over 6 cm or caecum over 9 cm is dilated; gas in the rectum argues against complete mechanical obstruction; sigmoid volvulus: inverted U-shaped loop from the pelvis, coffee bean sign, often treated with a flatus tube; Rigler's sign of free gas

sources.name: Tian BWCA, Vigutto G, Tan E, et al. WSES consensus guidelines on sigmoid volvulus management. World J Emerg Surg 2023;18:34
sources.supports: History, examination and full bloods including blood gas and lactate; ischaemia may be present without a raised lactate (rec 1); plain radiograph first, coffee bean sign (rec 2); CT if the diagnosis is in doubt or ischaemia or perforation suspected (rec 3); flexible endoscopic decompression first line if no ischaemia or perforation (rec 4), effective in 60-95%; view the mucosa and leave a decompression flatus tube; urgent resection if detorsion fails or the colon is non-viable or perforated (rec 5); after decompression offer sigmoid colectomy, as early as possible, even on the index admission (rec 6); recurrence 43-75% after detorsion; endoscopic fixation in selected patients at prohibitive risk (rec 8)

partner.opening: I'll read out Mr Finch's abdominal X-ray findings. Please interpret them.

reveals.finding: Read out: supine abdominal radiograph of Mr Albert Finch, taken today, covering the diaphragm to the symphysis pubis. A single, massively dilated loop of bowel, about 12 cm across and with no haustral markings, rises out of the pelvis in an inverted-U shape, its apex lying high in the right upper quadrant. Its two limbs lie side by side, and their adjoining walls form a dense line running down towards the pelvis. The rest of the colon is dilated, with haustra visible. No free intraperitoneal gas is seen.

reveals.trigger: Asks how to tell small from large bowel
reveals.finding: Read out, for comparison: in a second patient, the supine film shows several dilated loops of bowel up to 4 cm wide in the centre of the abdomen, with fine folds crossing the full width of each loop; little or no gas is seen in the colon. In a third patient, dilated bowel up to 8 cm wide lies around the periphery of the abdomen, with folds crossing only partway across; the caecum measures 10 cm, and there is no single inverted-U loop.
Grossly distended, tympanic, mildly tender, no guarding or rebound. Empty rectum.

reveals.trigger: Asks for bloods and a gas
reveals.finding: WCC 11.2, CRP 38, creatinine 104, K 3.4; lactate 1.6 mmol/L, pH 7.39.
Say: "The loop untwists with a rush of gas; the mucosa is pink."

push.question: What features tell you this is sigmoid volvulus?
push.expect: Featureless inverted-U loop from the pelvis, coffee bean sign, proximal colon dilated.

push.question: Why not go straight to theatre?
push.expect: No ischaemia or perforation: endoscopic decompression first, effective in 60–95%.

push.question: He's decompressed. What next?
push.expect: Recurrence 43–75%: offer sigmoid colectomy, ideally on this admission.

curveballs.prompt: At sigmoidoscopy the mucosa is black.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Non-viable colon: withdraw, resuscitate, consultant, and urgent resection.

curveballs.prompt: The erect chest film shows free gas under the diaphragm.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Perforation: no endoscopy; resuscitate, antibiotics, and theatre.

curveballs.prompt: He has severe dementia and a treatment escalation plan limiting surgery.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Decompress; discuss with family and consultant; endoscopic fixation or a palliative plan if surgery is too risky.
